# Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths

Haori Lu ^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding author.    Tianyu Gao    Yaoyao
Liu    Yingying Li Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Affiliation: {haorilu2, tianyu30, lyy, yl101}@illinois.edu

###### Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact
with environments and improve their decisions during deployment.
However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated
interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains
underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model
Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch
predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the
agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes
with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being
executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither
explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for
task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs
guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables
self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and
action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation
prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three
backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and
the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will
be made publicly available.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents interact with environments by
interpreting observations and taking actions to accomplish tasks.
Long-horizon tasks require them to sustain progress under incomplete
observations, where poor decisions can lead to repeated failures or
wasted interactions. Building agents that make reliable decisions over
extended interactions therefore remains a central challenge.

Prior work improves interactive decision making in several complementary
ways. ReAct interleaves reasoning with environment feedback ([Yao
et al., 2023b](#bib.bib53)), but commits to a single proposed action at
each step, which may miss useful alternatives. Search-based methods
instead explore multiple reasoning or action paths at inference
time ([Yao et al., 2023a](#bib.bib52); [Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib58);
[Hao et al., 2023](#bib.bib10); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), but
their cost grows with the breadth and depth of the search. A separate
line improves agents through retrieved reflections and
trajectory-derived action advantages ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib35);
[Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib14)). These directions motivate exploring a
few alternatives before acting, without executing them, together with
experience gathered through interaction. This also resembles how people
mentally simulate a few alternatives before choosing ([Gilbert and
Wilson, 2007](#bib.bib7); [Vul et al., 2014](#bib.bib41)): the agent
imagines the outcomes of several candidate actions ([Hafner et al.,
2020](#bib.bib9); [Gu et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)), which avoids the
interaction steps and potential irreversible consequences of trying them
in the environment. Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control offers
a concrete recipe for this pattern: it samples a finite batch of
candidate trajectories, weights them by predicted costs with exponential
(Gibbs) weights, executes only the next action, and replans ([Williams
et al., 2015](#bib.bib46); [Williams et al., 2017](#bib.bib47)).

Language environments, however, provide neither explicit dynamics nor
costs. A language world model can supply the missing dynamics by
predicting the outcome of each candidate action ([Hao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib10); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56)), but better next-observation prediction does not
necessarily yield higher task success ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56)). We therefore couple prediction directly with
decision making: the agent predicts the outcomes of several candidate
actions, an evaluator assigns costs for task progress and risk, and
MPPI-style weights summarize these costs for a final controller that
selects or synthesizes the action to execute.

To make both the candidates and their predictions more reliable over
time, we further introduce a dual-branch experience memory for
self-improvement. The planner branch uses accumulated experience to
improve candidate generation and action selection, while the world model
branch improves next-observation prediction, so that a single stream of
interaction experience improves both what is proposed and what is
predicted. Both branches operate through retrieved textual context, with
policy and world model parameters frozen. Our analysis bounds the
agent’s per-step regret in terms of three error sources, namely limited
candidate coverage, errors in action selection, and inaccurate
next-observation predictions, which motivates the two branches.

Experiments on ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib36)) and
ScienceWorld ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib43)) demonstrate the strongest
overall success-rate performance among the evaluated methods across
three backbones. Our main contributions are:

- •
  We propose a test-time, MPPI-inspired framework that improves a
  bounded predict–select–replan decision loop with experience: a world
  model predicts the outcomes of a few candidate actions, and a
  dual-branch memory improves both candidate generation and selection
  and next-observation prediction.
- •
  We provide a theoretical analysis showing that the weighting rule is
  optimal under a KL-regularized objective, and that the per-step regret
  is bounded in terms of candidate coverage, action selection, and
  next-observation prediction errors, which motivates the two memory
  branches.
- •
  Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones
  demonstrate the strongest overall success rate performance among
  baselines. We also provide ablation studies and a computational cost
  analysis.

## 2 Related Work

#### LLM agents.

LLM agents choose actions from textual or visual observations ([Wu
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib48); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib49)) in a loop.
ReAct ([Yao et al., 2023b](#bib.bib53)) and SayCan ([Ahn et al.,
2022](#bib.bib1)) ground actions in environmental feedback or available
skills, ADaPT ([Prasad et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)) decomposes tasks, and
further methods support lookahead through branching or retrieved
information ([Yao et al., 2023a](#bib.bib52); [Zhou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib58); [Koh et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Holt et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). In traditional control, a related perspective also
uses lookahead: model-predictive control ([Camacho and Bordons,
2007](#bib.bib3)) plans over a finite horizon, executes only the first
action, and replans from the new observation. MPPI further weights
sampled trajectories by their predicted costs ([Williams et al.,
2015](#bib.bib46); [Williams et al., 2017](#bib.bib47)). We adapt MPPI’s
strategy of predicting and weighting multiple candidates to language
agents through world model prediction, replacing its continuous control
update with a discrete action update driven by language models, and thus
call our framework MPPI-inspired.

#### World models for agent planning.

World models can estimate how actions change an environment before they
are executed. Dynalang ([Lin et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), RAP ([Hao
et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)), WebDreamer ([Gu et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)),
and IMPLEMENT ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)) simulate action outcomes
with language-based or lightweight world models; while ITP ([Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)), WKM ([Qiao et al., 2024](#bib.bib32)), and
WorldEvolver ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib56)) add adaptive lookahead,
structured knowledge, or retrieved experience. Qian et al. ([Qian
et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)) and Li et al. ([Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib18)) study how well agents use forecasts and whether LLMs
can serve as text-based world models. More recently, MemWM ([Wang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)) trains a world model with offline-built
memory to evaluate the candidates. Unlike them, we keep all models
frozen and use experience gathered during interaction in two branches
that improve next-observation prediction and candidate generation and
selection.

#### Self-improving agents.

Experience-based methods improve later decisions by retaining
information from prior interactions, building on memory systems ([Park
et al., 2023](#bib.bib29); [Packer et al., 2023](#bib.bib28); [Chhikara
et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib51); [Sumers et al.,
2024](#bib.bib38); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib20); [Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21); [Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)). Reflexion ([Shinn
et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)), ExpeL ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib57)),
ERL ([Allard et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)), and ReasoningBank ([Ouyang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)) distill feedback or trajectories into
experience, Voyager ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib42)) and AWM ([Wang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)) retain skills or task procedures,
AdaPlanner ([Sun et al., 2023](#bib.bib39)) and JitRL ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib14)) revise plans or action preferences from retrieved
experience, and Memento ([Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib59)), ACE ([Zhang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)), and Dynamic Cheatsheet ([Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)) adapt through episodic memory or evolving contexts
instead of fine-tuning ([Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)). These methods
improve what the agent proposes; our dual-branch memory also improves
what it predicts, so a single stream of interaction experience sharpens
both the candidates and the forecasts used to choose among them.

![Refer to caption](2610.28945v1/method.png)

Figure 1: Overview of our method. At step $`t`$, the proposal policy
takes the goal, history, and observation and proposes $`K`$ candidate
actions $`a_{t}^{(k)}`$. The world model predicts the next observation
$`\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)}`$ of each candidate, the evaluator scores task
progress and risk to give costs $`C_{t}^{(k)}`$, and MPPI-style weights
summarize these costs for the final controller, which decides the
executed action $`a_{t}`$. After execution, the transition updates both
experience branches. The planner branch labels it as success, failure,
or ignore and summarizes the first two into $`M_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}}`$
and $`M_{t}^{\mathrm{final}}`$, retrieved by the proposal policy and
final controller in future steps; the world model branch updates its
episodic and semantic memory $`M_{t}^{\mathrm{world}}`$, retrieved by
the world model in future steps.

## 3 Problem Formulation

We consider a language agent solving a long-horizon interactive task
with goal $`g`$ and an interaction budget of $`T`$ steps. At step $`t`$,
the agent receives an observation $`o_{t}`$ and has interaction history
$`h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1})`$. It acts from context
$`x_{t}=(g,h_{t},o_{t})`$. Its policy $`\pi(\cdot\mid x_{t})`$ defines a
distribution over language actions, and the action at step $`t`$ is
generated according to:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}.
       ```                                                        |     | (1) |

After $`a_{t}`$ is applied, the environment generates the next
observation according to:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       o_{t+1}\sim P_{\mathrm{env}}(o^{\prime}\mid h_{t},o_{t},a_{t}).
       ```                                                              |     | (2) |

Our objective is to maximize the probability of completing the task
within the interaction budget:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \pi^{\star}=\arg\max_{\pi}\Pr(\text{success by }T\mid g,\pi).
       ```                                                            |     | (3) |

In control, Model-Predictive Control (MPC) plans over a finite horizon
$`H`$ by selecting the candidate action sequence
$`\mathbf{a}=(a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1})`$ with the lowest expected
predicted cost:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathbf{a}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{a}}\bar{J}_{t}(\mathbf{a}),
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\bar{J}_{t}`$ is the expected cost of the model-predicted
trajectory ([Camacho and Bordons, 2007](#bib.bib3); [Rawlings et al.,
2017](#bib.bib34); [Li et al., 2019](#bib.bib15); [Li et al.,
2020](#bib.bib17); [Zhang et al., 2021](#bib.bib55); [Li et al.,
2021](#bib.bib16)). MPC executes only the first action and replans after
the next observation. Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) ([Williams
et al., 2015](#bib.bib46); [Williams et al., 2017](#bib.bib47))
approximates this search by sampling candidate trajectories and favoring
those with lower predicted costs with Gibbs weights. This
predict-and-replan cycle suits our agent tasks, where each action shapes
later decisions. Inspired by MPPI, we develop a test-time framework for
language agents that uses a world model to evaluate multiple candidate
actions and guide decision-making. The next section presents our method
in detail.

## 4 Method

We first describe the test-time loop: a world model predicts outcomes
for up to $`K`$ proposed actions, and MPPI-inspired weighting of
task-conditioned costs guides a final controller to select or synthesize
an action before replanning from the new observation. We then describe
how dual-branch experience memory improves planning and grounds future
forecasts.

### 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop

At time step $`t`$, the agent receives the goal, interaction history,
current observation, and action protocol. Let $`M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}}`$
denote the planner experiences retrieved for this decision, which will
be introduced in
Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
in detail. The proposal module first reasons over the context, and then
emits up to $`K`$ atomic candidate actions. The resulting candidate set
is represented as:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{a_{t}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N_{t}},`$ | $`\displaystyle 1\leq N_{t}\leq K,`$ |  | (5) |
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{t}^{(k)}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim q_{\pi}(a\mid x_{t},M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}}),`$ | $`\displaystyle k=1,\ldots,N_{t}.`$ |  |  |

Here $`q_{\pi}`$ denotes the proposal policy, $`K`$ is the maximum
number of candidates, and $`N_{t}`$ is the number generated at step
$`t`$. This adapts MPPI’s candidate sampling to language actions:
instead of adding perturbations to a continuous control sequence, the
proposal policy generates candidate actions that could advance the task,
gather information, or recover from failures.

Next, for each proposal, the world model receives the goal, current
observation, candidate action, and retrieved world model memory
$`M_{t}^{\mathrm{world}}`$.

It predicts a one-step textual observation of the action’s immediate
consequence:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)}\sim\hat{P}(o^{\prime}\mid g,o_{t},a_{t}^{(k)},M_{t}^{\mathrm{world}}).
``` |  | (6) |

We use one-step prediction rather than multi-step rollouts to simplify
the architecture and control computational cost. We denote the resulting
candidate-specific imagined transition by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{\tau}_{t}^{(k)}=(g,h_{t},o_{t},a_{t}^{(k)},\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)}),
``` |  | (7) |

which bundles the task context, proposed action, and predicted outcome
used to evaluate that candidate. In classical MPPI, candidate
trajectories are evaluated by a numerical cost function. For language
agents, we instantiate this cost-evaluation stage through textual
outcome prediction and evaluation of task progress and risk. A language
evaluator maps each imagined transition to a bounded predictive cost:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{t}^{(k)}=C_{\psi}(g,h_{t},o_{t},a_{t}^{(k)},\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)})\in[0,100],
``` |  | (8) |

where lower cost indicates greater predicted usefulness for the goal.
The evaluator considers expected task progress, information value, and
whether the predicted outcomes are consistent with the available
evidence. To account for uncertainty in predicted costs, we optimize a
distribution $`\mathbf{w}`$ that favors low-cost candidates while
retaining alternatives. We denote its regularized objective by
$`\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w})`$ and its minimizing distribution by
$`\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}`$; the objective combines weighted predictive
cost with a KL penalty from uniform weighting.

###### Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting).

For $`N_{t}\geq 1`$ candidates with finite costs, let $`\Delta_{N_{t}}`$
denote the probability simplex and $`u_{t}^{(k)}=1/N_{t}`$ the uniform
reference. For $`\lambda>0`$, consider

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\Delta_{N_{t}}}\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w}),`$ |  | (9) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{t}}w^{(k)}C_{t}^{(k)}+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{w}\|\mathbf{u}_{t}),`$ |  |  |

The objective has a unique minimizer

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w_{t}^{(k)\star}=\frac{\exp(-C_{t}^{(k)}/\lambda)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_{t}}\exp(-C_{t}^{(j)}/\lambda)}.
``` |  | (10) |

For every $`\mathbf{w}\in\Delta_{N_{t}}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w})-\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})=\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{w}\|\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})\geq 0.
``` |  | (11) |

The minimizing distribution is the standard Gibbs cost-tilted form
underlying MPPI ([Williams et al., 2017](#bib.bib47)), which also admits
a free-energy interpretation of bounded-rational choice ([Ortega and
Braun, 2013](#bib.bib26)). The proof is in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Theoretical Analysis and Proofs ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").
Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
shows that candidate weights depend on cost differences scaled by
$`\lambda`$: smaller $`\lambda`$ emphasizes the lowest predicted costs,
whereas larger $`\lambda`$ retains more balanced influence across
candidates. Our main configuration uses $`\lambda=10`$. We use
$`w_{t}^{(k)}=w_{t}^{(k)\star}`$ below. The weights then guide the final
controller, which also receives the goal, trajectory, observation,
candidate set, predicted outcomes, and retrieved planner experiences. We
denote its action-generation step by

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{(\hat{o}_{t+1}^{(k)},w_{t}^{(k)})\}_{k=1}^{N_{t}},`$ |  | (12) |
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\mathrm{final}}(\cdot\mid x_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t},M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}}),`$ |  |  |

where $`\pi_{\mathrm{final}}`$ is the final controller. It generates an
action, selecting a proposed action or synthesizing a new atomic action
when useful. The controller executes only the selected action in the
real environment. It then appends the resulting observation to the
trajectory and repeats the process from the updated context.

### 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory

The weighting in
Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
depends on both the proposed actions and the accuracy of their predicted
costs. It cannot assign weight to a useful action absent from the
candidate set, and inaccurate forecasts can favor unsuitable candidates.
Moreover, optimal candidate weights do not guarantee an optimal final
action, since action selection is performed by a separate controller.
Our dual-branch memory aligns with these limitations: the planner branch
targets candidate coverage and final action selection, while the world
model branch adapts forecasts to environment-specific dynamics.

###### Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection).

Fix a nonempty candidate set, its uniform reference $`\mathbf{u}_{t}`$,
and $`\lambda>0`$. Let $`\bar{C}_{t}(a)`$ denote a reference cost for
any action $`a`$, with $`\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}=\bar{C}_{t}(a_{t}^{(k)})`$,
and let $`\mathbf{C}_{t}`$ be the predictive costs, with

|     |                                                      |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \max_{k}|C_{t}^{(k)}-\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}|\leq\epsilon.
       ```                                                   |     | (13) |

Define $`\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}`$ by replacing $`\mathbf{C}_{t}`$ with
$`\bar{\mathbf{C}}_{t}`$ in
Eq. ([9](#S4.E9 "In Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")),
and let $`\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t}`$ minimize $`\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}`$. The
predictive weights $`\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}`$ satisfy

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})-\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq 2\epsilon,`$ |  | (14) |
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}\|\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{2\epsilon}{\lambda}.`$ |  | (15) |

Moreover, for any comparator action $`a^{\circ}`$, possibly outside the
candidate set, define the coverage gap and the selection gap

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{cov}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\min_{k}\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}-\bar{C}_{t}(a^{\circ}),`$ |  | (16) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{final}}}\big[\bar{C}_{t}(a_{t})\big]-\sum_{k=1}^{N_{t}}w_{t}^{(k)\star}\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)},`$ |  | (17) |

where the expectation is over the controller’s output given its inputs
in
Eq. ([12](#S4.E12 "In 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")).
Then the executed action satisfies

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{final}}}\big[\bar{C}_{t}(a_{t})\big]-\bar{C}_{t}(a^{\circ})`$ |  | (18) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\underbrace{\delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}}_{\text{selection}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{cov}}}_{\text{coverage}}+\underbrace{2\epsilon}_{\text{cost error}}+\underbrace{\lambda\log N_{t}}_{\text{temperature}}.`$ |  |  |

The proof is in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Theoretical Analysis and Proofs ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").
Reference costs represent an ideal assessment of actual action
consequences, which are not available to the agent. Taking $`a^{\circ}`$
to be a reference-optimal action makes the left-hand side of
Eq. ([18](#S4.E18 "In Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths"))
a per-step regret and $`\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{cov}}\geq 0`$.
Eq. ([18](#S4.E18 "In Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths"))
separates the limitations above: the coverage gap is positive only when
a better action than every candidate exists, and shrinks as better
candidates are proposed, while $`\epsilon`$ decreases with more accurate
forecasts and cost assessments. The selection gap compares the
controller’s choice with the weighted candidates: it is negative when
the controller corrects inaccurate weights or generates a better action,
and positive when it disregards reliable guidance. This decomposition
guides our memory design. Candidate-generation memories target
$`\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{cov}}`$, final-planner memories target
$`\delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}`$, and world model memories target
$`\epsilon`$. Both memory branches update textual memories while keeping
the model parameters frozen.

#### Planner branch.

After each real transition, an experience extraction module labels the
step as SUCCESS, FAILURE, or IGNORE based on the observed outcome. It
then records experience only for SUCCESS and FAILURE, producing separate
summaries for candidate generation and final action selection. Each
memory bank $`\mathcal{W}_{d,y}`$ retains its most recent $`C`$ records.
To retrieve memories, let $`\mathcal{T}(\cdot)`$ map text to its set of
lowercase alphanumeric tokens, and let
$`\mathcal{Q}_{t}=\mathcal{T}(g)\cup\mathcal{T}(o_{t})`$ be the query
tokens. We score each memory $`m`$ by token-set Jaccard similarity and
keep the $`R`$ highest-scoring ones:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle s_{t}(m)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{|\mathcal{T}(m)\cap\mathcal{Q}_{t}|}{|\mathcal{T}(m)\cup\mathcal{Q}_{t}|},`$ |  | (19) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{d,y,t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname*{top\text{-}\mathit{R}}_{m\in\mathcal{W}_{d,y}}s_{t}(m),`$ |  |  |

where $`d\in\{\mathrm{cand},\mathrm{final}\}`$ indexes
candidate-generation or final-planner experiences, and
$`y\in\{\mathrm{success},\mathrm{failure}\}`$ indexes memory banks for
experiences from successful and failed steps. Accordingly, the planner
experiences in
Eqs. ([5](#S4.E5 "In 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths"))
and ([12](#S4.E12 "In 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths"))
are
$`M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}}=(M_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}},M_{t}^{\mathrm{final}})`$,
where $`M_{t}^{d}=\bigcup_{y}\mathcal{R}_{d,y,t}`$; the proposal policy
conditions on $`M_{t}^{\mathrm{cand}}`$ and the final controller on
$`M_{t}^{\mathrm{final}}`$.

three backbones, reported as SR@1 and SR@5. Bold and underlined success
rates indicate the best and second-best results, respectively.

#### World model branch.

For the world model branch, we adopt the episodic and semantic memory
design of WorldEvolver ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib56)), which we use
to reduce the predictive cost error $`\epsilon`$ in
Proposition [2](#Thmproposition2 "Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").
To support prediction for multiple candidate actions, we retrieve
relevant transitions separately for each candidate and use them with
shared environment rules to predict next observations. Memory is updated
only after real interaction, storing observed transitions and extracting
rules from prediction errors. The implementation details are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A World Model Memory Implementation Details ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

#### Benchmarks.

We evaluate our method on ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib36))
and ScienceWorld ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib43)) provided by
AgentBoard ([Ma et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)). Our evaluation includes 134
ALFWorld tasks and 90 ScienceWorld tasks, with each trial limited to 30
environment steps. ALFWorld is a text-based household benchmark of tasks
such as picking up, cleaning, heating, and moving objects, while
ScienceWorld is a text-based science benchmark where agents manipulate
objects and carry out simple experiments. Our primary metrics are SR@1,
the fraction of tasks solved in a single trial, and SR@5, the fraction
solved in at least one of five trials.

#### Baselines.

We compare our method with multiple baselines. ReAct ([Yao et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib53)) interleaves reasoning and action, using environment
observations to guide subsequent decisions. ITP-I, the training-free
variant of Imagine-then-Plan ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), uses
adaptive lookahead to imagine future outcomes and guide action
selection. WorldEvolver ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib56)) represents an
evolving language world model pipeline that uses episodic and semantic
experience. All baselines use the same task files and backbone.

#### Implementation details.

At each step, the agent generates up to $`K=8`$ candidate actions and
applies MPPI-style weighting with $`\lambda=10`$ to their predicted
costs. Candidate generation and final planning read from the
corresponding planner memory bank with capacity $`C=24`$ and retrieval
count $`R=4`$. The policy and world model parameters remain frozen
during deployment. Following WorldEvolver ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56)), we do not reset memory within each evaluation
setting. World model memory hyperparameters and prompt templates are in
Appendices [A](#A1 "Appendix A World Model Memory Implementation Details ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
and [D](#A4 "Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").
We also vary the backbone, evaluating Gemma-4-26B-A4B ([Gemma Team,
2026](#bib.bib6)), Qwen3.5-9B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib33)), and
GPT-5.4-mini ([OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib25)), to test generalization across
models. In all tables, bold and underlined numbers mark the best and
second-best results per column, shaded rows are the default setting, and
Avg. is the mean over ALFWorld and ScienceWorld.

### 5.2 Results

#### Results on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld.

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Planner branch. ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
compares our method with ReAct, ITP-I, and WorldEvolver on ALFWorld and
ScienceWorld across three backbones. With Gemma-4-26B-A4B, Ours leads on
both benchmarks, scoring 65.7/84.3 on ALFWorld and 46.7/60.0 on
ScienceWorld, and improves over the strongest baseline, ITP-I, by
32.9/29.8 and 10.0/10.0 points, respectively. With Qwen3.5-9B and
GPT-5.4-mini, Ours achieves the best ALFWorld results and remains
competitive on ScienceWorld: it ranks second behind ReAct on Qwen3.5-9B,
and leads in SR@1 but ranks second in SR@5 on GPT-5.4-mini. Across the
three backbones, Ours achieves the strongest overall performance,
ranking first in nine comparisons and second in the remaining three.
Per-task ALFWorld results are reported in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Detailed Results ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").

Figure 2: Executed actions by candidate rank under MPPI-style weighting
with Gemma-4-26B-A4B. Rank 1 includes ties for the highest weight;
Outside denotes actions not in the proposal set.

#### Action selection analysis.

Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Results on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld. ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
shows that the controller selects a highest-weight candidate in
77.8–83.8% of decisions across both benchmarks and trial settings.
Second-ranked candidates account for 10.4–12.2%, while actions outside
the proposal set account for 1.6–6.0%. The controller therefore usually
follows the highest-weight candidate, while retaining the flexibility to
choose other candidates or generate new actions.

Figure 3: An example of how retrieved experience and predictive
evaluation guide action selection. Our agent completes the focus subgoal
before pickup and succeeds, while ReAct skips this subgoal and fails.

#### Illustrative example.

Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Action selection analysis. ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
shows how retrieved experience and predictive scoring guide a
ScienceWorld trajectory. At Step 4, retrieved experience identifies
focusing on the target as a prerequisite for pickup, and the controller
selects the lower-cost focus action over immediate pickup. After this
subgoal is completed, the predicted cost of pickup falls from 40 to 10,
making it the preferred action at Step 5 and leading to
environment-verified success with a score of 100. In contrast, ReAct
skips the focus subgoal and repeatedly declares completion despite
ending with failure.

### 5.3 Ablation Study

#### Action candidate number $`K`$.

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Action candidate number 𝐾. ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
evaluates candidate-set sizes $`K\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}`$. The default
$`K=8`$ gives the highest SR@1 on both benchmarks, exceeding $`K=1`$ by
5.3 percentage points on ALFWorld and 3.4 points on ScienceWorld. Larger
sets help SR@5 only on ScienceWorld, where $`K=16`$ raises it from 60.0
to 68.9 while SR@1 declines, possibly because of its larger and more
varied action space. Since larger candidate sets do not consistently
help, we use $`K=8`$ in all settings as a moderate choice that balances
candidate coverage and cost.

| $`K`$ | ALFWorld |      | ScienceWorld |      | Avg. |      |
|-------|----------|------|--------------|------|------|------|
|       | SR@1     | SR@5 | SR@1         | SR@5 | SR@1 | SR@5 |
| 1     | 60.4     | 82.1 | 43.3         | 58.9 | 51.9 | 70.5 |
| 2     | 59.7     | 85.1 | 38.9         | 56.7 | 49.3 | 70.9 |
| 4     | 61.9     | 82.8 | 40.0         | 58.9 | 51.0 | 70.9 |
| 8     | 65.7     | 84.3 | 46.7         | 60.0 | 56.2 | 72.2 |
| 16    | 64.2     | 84.3 | 42.2         | 68.9 | 53.2 | 76.6 |

Table 2: Effect of the number of candidate actions $`K`$ imagined per
step, with Gemma-4-26B-A4B (%). The default setting is shaded.

#### Weight temperature $`\lambda`$.

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Weight temperature 𝜆. ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
evaluates $`\lambda\in\{1,10,50\}`$, where larger values produce flatter
weights and reduce the influence of predictive cost differences.
Performance is similar at $`\lambda=1`$ and $`\lambda=10`$, whereas
$`\lambda=50`$ degrades ALFWorld, lowering SR@1 from 65.7 to 53.7, and
ScienceWorld is less sensitive. We use $`\lambda=10`$ as the default, an
intermediate temperature that keeps cost differences informative while
softening the weights, and the results are not sensitive to this choice
between $`\lambda=1`$ and $`\lambda=10`$.

#### Experience ablations.

Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Experience ablations. ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
isolates the contributions of planner memory and world model memory.
Their effects differ across benchmarks: world model memory alone helps
on ALFWorld, raising SR@1 from 56.7 to 68.7, but hurts on ScienceWorld,
whereas planner memory alone helps on ScienceWorld but hurts on
ALFWorld. Enabling both branches achieves the highest average SR@1 and
SR@5, though the gains are not uniform across benchmarks. Figure 4 shows
cumulative SR@1 as tasks are executed: the two curves coincide on the
first tasks and then separate, with the gap persisting on both
benchmarks, consistent with experience accumulating across trajectories.
Experience also takes effect within a single trajectory, as shown in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Action selection analysis. ‣ 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths"),
where the experience summarized at one step is retrieved at the next.

### 5.4 Computational Cost

Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.4 Computational Cost ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
reports per-step latency measured on a task subset with Gemma-4-26B-A4B
running on 2$`\times`$ NVIDIA A40 GPUs. Our method takes 6.72 seconds
per step, compared with 0.51–1.94 seconds for the baselines. The
additional overhead comes from predicting and scoring multiple candidate
actions before execution. Although slower, this remains practical for
tasks without strict real-time constraints, where improved task success
can justify the added cost.

| Method | Avg. sec. / step$`\downarrow`$ | SR@1$`\uparrow`$ | SR@5$`\uparrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|
| ReAct | 0.51 | 20.1 | 24.6 |
| ITP-I | 1.94 | 32.8 | 54.5 |
| WorldEvolver | 1.33 | 16.4 | 20.9 |
| Ours | 6.72 | 65.7 | 84.3 |

2$`\times`$ NVIDIA A40 GPUs.

## 6 Conclusion

We presented a self-improving, test-time MPPI-inspired framework for
language agents performing long-horizon tasks. The framework predicts
the outcomes of several candidate actions with a world model before
acting, and uses MPPI-style weights to summarize their costs for the
final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables
self-improvement: planner memory refines candidate generation and
selection, and world model memory improves next-observation prediction.
Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld demonstrate the strongest
overall performance across three backbones, with measured computational
costs remaining practical for the evaluated tasks.

## 7 Limitations

First, world model accuracy is important because predicted outcomes
determine candidate costs and can change the controller’s action
preference. Our current dual-branch adaptation relies on retrieved
textual experience while keeping model parameters frozen. More capable
mechanisms for improving world model accuracy and adapting to changing
dynamics remain an important direction for future work. Second,
evaluating multiple candidates requires additional world model and
evaluator calls at test time. This increases inference latency and cost
as the candidate set grows, motivating more computationally efficient
ways to obtain useful candidate comparisons.

Ethical considerations. Our experiments are conducted entirely in
text-based simulated environments and involve no human subjects or
personal data. If such an agent were deployed in real environments,
inaccurate world model predictions could lead to unsafe actions, so
human oversight would be needed.

## Appendix A World Model Memory Implementation Details

Our implementation adopts WorldEvolver’s episodic and semantic memory
design ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib56)) as auxiliary prediction
context. For each real transition, the episodic bank stores the current
observation, executed action, and observation returned by the
environment. For a candidate action $`a`$, we tokenize it and each
stored action $`a^{\prime}`$ into token sets and score them by Jaccard
similarity:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s(a,a^{\prime})=\frac{|\mathcal{T}(a)\cap\mathcal{T}(a^{\prime})|}{|\mathcal{T}(a)\cup\mathcal{T}(a^{\prime})|}.
``` |  |

We retrieve up to the five highest-scoring transitions. Each retrieved
record is presented as a state–action–next-state example. The predictor
prompt also includes the task goal and current observation.

The semantic memory bank stores reusable rules about environment changes
and persistence. For each prediction–observation mismatch, the language
model extracts at most one rule. Up to eight recent rules guide
subsequent predictions.

For both benchmarks, the episodic memory bank stores up to 100
transitions and retrieves up to 5 per candidate, while the semantic
memory bank stores up to 128 rules and supplies up to 8 per prediction.
Memory is retained across trajectories within each environment, allowing
later interactions to reuse accumulated experience.

## Appendix B Theoretical Analysis and Proofs

We prove
Propositions [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
and [2](#Thmproposition2 "Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").

###### Proof of Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").

Suppress the time index and define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle Z`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{N}u^{(k)}\exp(-C^{(k)}/\lambda),`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle w^{(k)\star}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{u^{(k)}\exp(-C^{(k)}/\lambda)}{Z}.`$ |  |

Since $`u^{(k)}=1/N`$, these weights coincide with
Eq. ([10](#S4.E10 "In Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")).
Using

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \log\frac{w^{(k)\star}}{u^{(k)}}=-\frac{C^{(k)}}{\lambda}-\log Z,
       ```                                                                |     |

we obtain

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{w})=\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{w}\|\mathbf{w}^{\star})-\lambda\log Z.
``` |  |

The KL divergence is nonnegative and vanishes only at
$`\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}^{\star}`$, establishing the unique minimizer.
Since $`\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{w}^{\star})=-\lambda\log Z`$, subtracting
this minimum gives the stated identity. We use the convention
$`0\log 0=0`$. ∎

###### Proof of Proposition [2](#Thmproposition2 "Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths").

For any distribution $`\mathbf{w}`$ on the fixed candidate set, the
cost-error assumption implies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w})-\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\mathbf{w})|\leq\sum_{k}w^{(k)}\epsilon=\epsilon.
``` |  |

Optimality of $`\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}`$ for $`\mathcal{F}_{t}`$ then
gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{F}_{t}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})+\epsilon`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{F}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})+\epsilon`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})+2\epsilon.`$ |  |

This proves
Eq. ([14](#S4.E14 "In Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")).
Applying
Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
to the reference costs gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star})-\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}\|\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})\leq 2\epsilon.`$ |  |

Dividing by $`\lambda>0`$ establishes
Eq. ([15](#S4.E15 "In Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")).

For
Eq. ([18](#S4.E18 "In Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")),
nonnegativity of the KL term gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{k}w_{t}^{(k)\star}\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}\leq\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\star}).
``` |  |

The proof of
Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Optimal candidate weighting). ‣ 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")
also gives
$`\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})=-\lambda\log\bar{Z}_{t}`$,
where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\bar{Z}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{t}}\sum_{k}\exp(-\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}/\lambda)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{N_{t}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\min_{k}\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}}{\lambda}\right).`$ |  |

Therefore,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t})\leq\min_{k}\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}+\lambda\log N_{t}.
``` |  |

Combining these inequalities with
Eq. ([14](#S4.E14 "In Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths"))
yields

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{k}w_{t}^{(k)\star}\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}\leq\min_{k}\bar{C}_{t}^{(k)}+2\epsilon+\lambda\log N_{t}.
``` |  |

Adding $`\delta_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}`$ to both sides turns the left-hand
side into
$`\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{final}}}[\bar{C}_{t}(a_{t})]`$,
where the expectation is over
$`a_{t}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{final}}(\cdot\mid x_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t},M_{t}^{\mathrm{P}})`$
in
Eq. ([12](#S4.E12 "In 4.1 MPPI-Inspired Decision Loop ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths")).
Subtracting $`\bar{C}_{t}(a^{\circ})`$ then yields
Eq. ([18](#S4.E18 "In Proposition 2 (Coverage, cost error, and selection). ‣ 4.2 Dual-Branch Experience Memory ‣ 4 Method ‣ Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths"))
by the definition of $`\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{cov}}`$. The selection gap
captures the final controller’s contribution to per-step regret,
completing the decomposition into candidate coverage, predictive cost
error, and action selection. ∎

## Appendix D Prompt Templates

We use WorldEvolver’s ReactAgent prompt ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56)) as a starting point and substantially revise it for
our framework. The resulting module-specific prompts are presented
below.

### D.1 Candidate Generation

Both calls receive the shared context below. Call 1 appends a reasoning
instruction; Call 2 appends the returned reasoning and
candidate-generation instructions.

#### Shared context.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Generate 1 to 8 distinct one-step action candidates.

Environment instruction:

{environment_instruction}

There is an interaction example (style and action/observation pattern
only; do not copy its final Thought/Action output contract):

{fixed_demonstration}

This stage proposes candidates for a

downstream planner. It does not execute an action and must use the
separate

candidate format at the end of this prompt.

Goal:

{goal}

Trajectory:

{trajectory}

Current observation:

{current_observation}

Learned planner experience (fallible; success and failure experiences):

- {retrieved_candidate_experience_1}

- {retrieved_candidate_experience_2}

- ...

Follow the public protocol exactly. Generate distinct one-step actions

that may reveal useful information or advance the task.

Prefer a grounded action that directly advances the goal.

Use an information action only when it can resolve relevant uncertainty.

Preserve the operation requested by the goal; do not replace it with an
unrelated

information action. If multiple visible referents are plausible, include
distinct

grounded alternatives.

Copy every non-empty argument verbatim from the current observation or
an environment Observation in the trajectory. Never use names found only
in the Goal, demonstrations, or earlier model-generated actions.

Do not repeat the latest unchanged failed action or add redundant
candidates.

Candidates are suggestions, not guarantees.

If no grounded argumented action is available, output one useful
zero-argument protocol action.

Keep candidates distinct and do not repeat the latest unchanged failure.

Return only:

CANDIDATE_1=\<action\>

CANDIDATE_2=\<action\>

...

#### Call 1: Reasoning.

Input: Shared context + the following reasoning instruction.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Analyze the visible evidence, protocol, goal, and learned planner
experience briefly.

This is a private advisory analysis for a separate emitter: do not
reproduce

instructions or demonstrations, and do not emit candidate markers or
actions.

#### Call 2: Candidate Action Generation.

Input: Shared context + the following.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Advisory analysis from the candidate reasoner:

{candidate_reasoning}

Before emitting, correct any analysis that replaced an executable goal

operation with information gathering. If the goal operation’s target is

uncertain, use the visible plausible referents as separate candidates;
do not

emit only information-gathering actions when the requested operation
itself

can test the visible referents.

Now emit the candidate proposals. Return up to the requested maximum
number of lines in exactly

this form, with no Thought, Action, explanation, markdown, or text after
the

last line:

CANDIDATE_1=\<one atomic action\>

CANDIDATE_2=\<one atomic action\>

...

### D.2 World Model Prediction

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\## Frame Axioms and Persistence Rules

- {semantic_rule_1}

- {semantic_rule_2}

{additional_semantic_rules}

\## Retrieved similar past transitions

Current state: {retrieved_state_1}

Action: {retrieved_action_1}

Next state: {retrieved_next_state_1}

{additional_retrieved_transitions}

You are a world model for the {environment_name} environment. Given the
agent’s current observation, its proposed action, and the task goal,
predict what the agent will observe next.

If a "## Frame Axioms and Persistence Rules" section appears above,
treat each rule as a constraint: do not predict any change to a property
the rules say does not change for the action being taken. Use the rules
to filter out spurious changes.

If a "## Retrieved similar past transitions" section is provided, use
those transitions as analogies for what can change after this action.
Let the retrieved transitions guide what changes, but keep the
prediction consistent with the current observation and task goal.

Output format: a single paragraph starting with "Prediction:" describing
the next observation in the style of the environment’s own text output.

Task: {goal}

State:

{world_model_observation}

Action: {candidate_action}

Prediction:

### D.3 Cost Evaluation

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Score all candidate actions jointly as decision evidence for an
embodied-agent planner.

Goal:

{goal}

Trajectory:

{trajectory}

Current observation:

{current_observation}

Candidates and their uncertain WM predictions:

Candidate 1: {candidate_action_1}

WM predicted next observation: {predicted_next_observation_1}

Candidate 2: {candidate_action_2}

WM predicted next observation: {predicted_next_observation_2}

{remaining_candidate_prediction_blocks}

Relevant planner memory (fallible):

{retrieved_final_planner_memory_json}

Assign each candidate a cost from 0 to 100. A lower cost means more
likely to make useful progress or reveal useful information for the
goal; 100 means very poor. Consider the current observation and
trajectory, expected progress, information value, and whether the
predicted result is consistent with the visible evidence. WM predictions
are uncertain suggestions, not facts.

Do not reject, filter, rewrite, or replace any action. Score every
candidate, including weak ones, in one response.

Return only one line per candidate, in the original order:

COST_1=\<number from 0 to 100\>

COST_2=\<number from 0 to 100\>

...

### D.4 Final Action Selection

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Choose the next action for an embodied agent.

Environment instruction:

{environment_instruction}

There is an interaction example (demonstrates
reasoning/action/observation style; the final output contract below
takes precedence):

{fixed_demonstration}

The environment instruction and example are references for this
decision. Use the candidates and forecasts supplied below, then follow
this planner’s final output contract.

Goal:

{goal}

Trajectory:

{trajectory}

Current observation:

{current_observation}

Candidate proposals and uncertain WM forecasts:

Candidate 1: {candidate_action_1}
